description:
Rajshahi team tackling Field Shift with NASA data and local farm knowledge. We plan a Bangla-English crop rotation planner with clear seasonal visuals. 

Kamruzzaman Khan Alve: Research and Data. Abid Al Hossain Swakkhar: App Development. Mahia Ribahna: Design and Video.
summary:
We developed Ritu (ঋতু, Bangla for "season"), a web app that helps smallholder farmers in Bangladesh plan a whole year of crops for each plot, not only the next one. A farmer pins the land on a map, adds plots, and says what grew there last year. Ritu compares year-long crop rotations and turns the chosen plan into a daily farm calendar.

Field Shift asks for tools that combine NASA Earth observations with local farming knowledge to build more resilient crop rotations. Ritu joins NASA POWER climate data, GPM IMERG rainfall and SMAP soil moisture with Bangladesh's national soil survey and local crop calendars. For each plan it shows irrigation need, heat risk, soil fit and dry-spell risk, and names the data behind every warning.

This matters because seasons are shifting: rain and heat are less predictable, one wrong crop can cost a farmer a season's income, and each season's crop limits what can grow next. Ritu shows these trade-offs in Bangla and English and leaves the final choice with the farmer. It is piloted in the Rajshahi region of Bangladesh, and the method can be extended to other regions as local crop and soil data are added.
details:
Live app: https://ritu-three.vercel.app

HOW IT WORKS

Ritu (ঋতু, Bangla for "season") helps smallholder farmers plan a whole year of crops for each plot, because what grows this season limits what can grow next.

1. The farmer pins the land on a map. Soil type and drainage are filled in from Bangladesh's national soil survey (BARC Crop Zoning) and can be corrected by the farmer.

2. The land is divided into plots. For each plot the farmer says how much irrigation water is available and what grew there last year.

3. Ritu uses NASA rainfall, temperature and soil-moisture data to compare year-long rotations across the three seasons (Rabi, Kharif-1, Kharif-2), drawn from 18 crops grown in the region, and explains in plain words why each plan suits that plot. Farmers can also build their own plan.

4. The chosen plan becomes a calendar: sowing windows, field jobs, irrigation with pump hours, and fertiliser amounts. The farmer can log notes and photos in a diary and set reminders.

NASA DATA:

- NASA POWER: long-term temperature and rainfall at the farm's location, used for each crop's water need, the number of irrigations, and heat risk.

- NASA GPM IMERG: daily satellite rainfall for 2001 to 2025, used to count how often a long dry spell has hit a crop's flowering and grain-filling weeks. This lowers a plan's score and adds a warning.

- NASA SMAP: root-zone soil moisture for 2015 to 2025, used to tell whether the soil is usually too dry at sowing, so the plan adds an irrigation before sowing.

Warnings name the dataset they come from, so the farmer and the extension officer can see the reason behind the advice.

BENEFITS

Ritu shows the trade-offs between rotations instead of giving one fixed answer, and the farmer keeps the final choice. It works in Bangla and English, needs no login, and keeps the farmer's records on their own device.

IMPACT

Our goal is to help farmers avoid crops that are likely to fail for lack of water or because of heat, use irrigation water more carefully, and keep soil productive across the year. Ritu is piloted in four districts of the Rajshahi region (Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Natore and Naogaon), and the method can be extended to other regions as local crop and soil data are added.

TOOLS

Next.js, React and TypeScript. NASA data came through the NASA POWER API and NASA Earthdata (OPeNDAP). Local data: BARC Crop Zoning, DAE BAMIS crop calendars, ISRIC SoilGrids, FAO ECOCROP, FAO-56, Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap. All sources are listed inside the app.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

Most crop tools advise on one crop at a time. Ritu treats the whole year as the unit of decision. It uses no trained model: every figure comes from counted NASA history and published crop requirements, so each recommendation can be traced and explained to the farmer.

DESIGN CHOICES

- Language and literacy: Bangla calendar months, local units, read-aloud, and pictures with labels.

- Trust: the app says "in this area", because NASA values describe a grid square, not one field.

- Honesty about limits: Ritu is a prototype and is decision support, not a replacement for local agricultural officers.

NEXT STEPS

Field testing with farmers and agriculture officers in Rajshahi, this week's NASA rainfall and soil moisture in the daily calendar, coverage of all of Bangladesh, and an offline mode with voice guidance.

USE OF AI (SI) TOOLS

Claude (Anthropic) was our main AI tool for planning, code, data-processing scripts and drafting text; OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity were used at times for code. Google Flow generated the illustrated video clips, which carry a visible "AI Generated" watermark. The team reviewed and tested all AI-written code. No AI or ML model makes the crop recommendations in the app.
